kurz: An emulsion is fat and water, which do not normally mix, held together as tiny droplets by a go-between.
bild_im_kopf: An [[emulgator|emulsifier]] is like an interpreter with one hand in the water and one in the fat. Without it, the two groups stand on opposite sides of the room.
was_passiert: Fat and water repel each other. Whisk hard, and the fat breaks into tiny droplets in the water. An emulsifier such as the lecithin in [[eigelb|egg yolk]] wraps around each droplet and stops them from flowing back together. The more densely packed the droplets, the thicker the sauce.
warum_wichtig: Mayonnaise, vinaigrette, hollandaise, [[beurre-blanc|beurre blanc]], pasta sauce with pasta water: all emulsions, all with the same pitfalls.
faustregeln: Add the fat drop by drop at first, later in a thin stream.
Bring ingredients to similar temperatures; nothing ice cold from the fridge.
[[senf|Mustard]], egg yolk or starchy pasta water help as go-betweens.
Split? Start again with a fresh yolk or a spoonful of water and slowly work in the split mixture.
typische_fehler: Hollandaise too hot, so the egg yolk sets.

praxis.text: A vinaigrette with a spoonful of mustard holds together much longer. Mayonnaise in a blender almost always works.
Pasta water brings starch, which binds fat and water in the pan into a creamy sauce.
Egg yolk is the classic emulsifier: a single yolk can carry a whole bowl of mayonnaise.

mythos.behauptung: Mayonnaise only works with eggs at room temperature.
mythos.richtig: Adding the oil slowly and whisking hard matter more. Similar temperatures help, but are not a must.
